title: Convolutional neural networks
matchup: LeCun et al. (1989) vs Fukushima (1979-80), Waibel et al. (1987-89) and Zhang et al. (1988)
question: Should the invention of the convolutional neural network be credited to Fukushima's neocognitron and to the backpropagation-trained networks of Waibel and Zhang, rather than to LeCun's 1989 network, as Schmidhuber says?

usual_credit.summary: Yann LeCun and colleagues at Bell Labs are usually credited with convolutional neural networks. Their 1989 paper trained a network with shared convolutional weights by backpropagation to read handwritten zip code digits, and the 1998 LeNet-5 paper spread the approach widely. The ACM's 2019 Turing Award announcement says LeCun developed convolutional networks in the 1980s and was the first to train one on images of handwritten digits.

claim.summary: Schmidhuber says the basic convolutional architecture with alternating convolution and downsampling layers is due to Fukushima's neocognitron of 1979-80, that Waibel combined convolutions, weight sharing and backpropagation in time-delay networks for speech in 1987, and that Zhang and colleagues trained a two-dimensional convolutional network by backpropagation to recognize characters in 1988. He says all of this came before LeCun's 1989 paper, that LeCun's papers and later surveys did not cite it, and that making CNNs work on a task should not outweigh inventing them.

response.summary: LeCun has said on X that the original Cognitron and Neocognitron did not use backpropagation because it had not yet been popularized, and that his 1989 network used strided convolutions where the neocognitron used separate simple-cell and complex-cell layers. He adds that Fukushima told him around 1991 that the 1989 paper had been a shock, and Nando de Freitas of DeepMind wrote that Fukushima avoided backpropagation on grounds of biological plausibility while LeCun trained neocognitron-style architectures with it. Jean-François Puget, who says he did his PhD in the same lab as a co-author of some early LeCun papers, replied to Schmidhuber that LeCun's work looked like an independent parallel track. The LeCun replies found for this case do not address the Zhang et al. paper specifically.

agreed_facts: Fukushima published the neocognitron in Biological Cybernetics in April 1980, after a Japanese version in 1979, and it was trained without backpropagation.

Waibel et al. published time-delay neural networks, one-dimensional convolutional networks trained by backpropagation for phoneme recognition, in IEEE Transactions on Acoustics, Speech, and Signal Processing in March 1989, following a 1987 report.

Zhang, Tanida, Itoh and Ichioka presented a backpropagation-trained shift-invariant network for character recognition in 1988 and published it in Applied Optics in 1990, with the manuscript received in April 1989.
LeCun et al. published 'Backpropagation Applied to Handwritten Zip Code Recognition' in Neural Computation 1(4) in 1989.
The ACM's 2019 Turing Award announcement says LeCun 'was the first to train a convolutional neural network system on images of handwritten digits'.
crux: Whether the 1989 LeCun et al. network counts as the invention of the CNN, or as the next step after Fukushima's architecture, Waibel's backpropagation-trained one-dimensional convolutions and Zhang et al.'s two-dimensional network, which the two sides weigh differently. A further question is whether LeCun knew of the Japanese work in 1988-89, which the sources reviewed do not establish.
